usage: Korean uses 만들다 (make), not 열다 (open), for accounts
to put money in the account
에 marks the account as the destination of the money
the account your monthly pay lands in; a fixed compound
사본 (寫本) = duplicate copy, often required for paperwork
examples: 통장 하나 만들고 싶어요.
I'd like to open one bank account.
하나 + 만들다 is the plain counter way to say 'open one'
월급이 통장에 들어왔어요.
My salary came into my account.
들어오다 (come in) is the verb for money arriving
회사에서 통장 사본을 달라고 했는데 어떻게 뽑아요?
My company asked for a copy of my bankbook — how do I print one?
real payroll-setup situation; 뽑다 = print out
nuance: 통장 (通帳, 'pass-through ledger') is literally the small paper passbook a bank prints transactions in, but in everyday speech it simply means your bank account — 월급 통장, 통장에 돈이 없어요. Its near-synonym 계좌 (口座) is the formal, technical word that appears on official forms and app menus; the dividing line is register, not meaning, and a crucial split shows up in compounds: the account NUMBER is always 계좌번호, never '통장번호'. Anyone, friend or banker, can say 통장 comfortably. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: don't pair it with 열다 ('open') as English does — Koreans 만들다 (make) a 통장 — and don't import 어카운트 or 'account number'; reach for 통장 in chat and 계좌번호 when reading out the digits.

Using 통장을 열다 by analogy with English 'open an account'; Koreans say 통장을 만들다.
Reaching for English 어카운트; in both casual and formal Korean the native word 통장/계좌 is expected.

usage: 로 marks the card as the means of payment
to be issued a debit card
발급받다 (發給) is the set verb for being issued a card/document
한도 (限度) here is capped by your balance, not by credit
for the debit card to not work
안 되다 is the everyday way to say a payment is declined
examples: 저는 보통 체크카드로 계산해요.
I usually pay with my debit card.
계산하다 (pay/settle) pairs naturally with 카드로
통장에 돈이 없어서 체크카드가 안 됐어요.
My debit card was declined because my account was empty.
shows the cause-and-effect: 체크카드 draws straight from the 통장
외국인등록증만 있으면 체크카드는 바로 발급받을 수 있어요.
If you just have your residence card, you can get a debit card issued on the spot.
real bank-counter situation for newcomers; ~만 있으면 = 'as long as you have'
nuance: 체크카드 is a debit card: the instant you pay, the money is pulled straight out of your linked 통장, so you can never spend more than you actually have. Compare it sharply with its partner 신용카드 (credit card), which lets you spend now and pay the bill next month — the dividing line is timing of the money, immediate withdrawal versus deferred billing. The word is a Konglish coinage ('check' + 카드) and is the only natural name; Koreans rarely say 데빗카드. Because issuance only requires a balance and no credit check, banks hand 체크카드 to recent arrivals easily, which is why most foreigners start here. The pitfall for English speakers is assuming any card offers a credit buffer — a 체크카드 has none, so '잔액이 부족하면' it simply declines.

usage: 긁다 (scratch) is the casual, slangy verb for paying by card
to apply for a credit card
신청하다 (申請) = formally apply, because issuance isn't automatic
명세서 (明細書) is the itemized monthly bill
할부 (割賦) = splitting a payment over months, a credit-only feature
examples: 이건 신용카드로 살게요.
I'll buy this with a credit card.
~로 살게요 is the simple checkout line
신용카드는 다음 달에 결제돼요.
The credit card gets charged next month.
결제되다 (be settled) captures the 'pay later' nature
외국인은 신용 기록이 없어서 신용카드 만들기가 좀 어려워요.
Since foreigners have no credit history, getting a credit card is a bit hard.
real newcomer hurdle; banks check your 신용 기록 (credit record)
nuance: 신용카드 (信用카드, 'trust-card') literally builds on 신용 — your creditworthiness, the bank's trust that you'll repay. You spend now and the total is 결제 (settled) next month, which is exactly what separates it from a 체크카드: the credit card defers the bill and depends on your 신용 record, while the debit card deducts instantly and needs none. Because that trust takes time to establish, banks routinely decline recent arrivals, so many residents carry a 체크카드 until they build a history. Natural collocations include 신용카드 할부 (installments) and 신용카드 명세서 (statement). The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 크레딧카드 — the native compound 신용카드 is universal — and remember the verb to apply is 신청하다, since unlike a debit card it is never issued on demand.

usage: 송금 + 하다 forms the verb; the object often takes 을/를 (돈을 송금하다)
해외 (海外) = abroad; the prototypical use of 송금
수수료 (手數料) is the service charge, steep on 해외 송금
안 되다 covers any failure to go through
examples: 친구한테 십만 원 송금했어요.
I transferred 100,000 won to my friend.
한테 marks the human recipient of the money
고향에 돈을 보내려면 해외 송금을 해야 해요.
To send money to my hometown, I have to do an overseas remittance.
~려면 = 'in order to'; pairs the casual 보내다 with the formal 송금
계좌번호만 알려 주시면 오늘 바로 송금해 드릴게요.
If you just give me the account number, I'll transfer it to you today.
real situation; 송금하다 needs a 계좌번호, and ~해 드릴게요 is polite service speech
nuance: 송금 (送金, literally 'send-money') is the act of sending funds to someone, near or far, and works as a verb with 하다. Its near-synonym is 이체 (account-to-account transfer): the dividing line is focus — 송금 foregrounds sending TO a person (친구한테 송금), while 이체 foregrounds the mechanical move BETWEEN accounts (계좌 이체). In casual domestic chat people often just say 돈 보내다, but 송금 sounds correct for bank wires and is the standard term for anything 해외 (overseas). Collocations: 해외 송금, 송금 수수료, 송금 한도. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing direction — 송금 is money going OUT (you send), whereas 입금 is money coming IN — and overlooking that 해외 송금 normally demands ID and a hefty 수수료.

Forgetting that 해외 송금 usually requires your ID and carries a real 수수료 (fee).
Marking the human recipient with 에 (the place particle); a person takes 에게/한테 — say 친구한테 송금했어요.

usage: the full set phrase you see on apps and ATMs
한도 (限度) = the daily cap on how much you can move
완료 (完了) is the confirmation wording inside banking apps
examples: 월세는 계좌 이체로 보내요.
I send the rent by bank transfer.
계좌 이체로 + 보내다 is the standard way to describe paying rent
하루 이체 한도가 넘어서 더는 못 보내요.
I've gone over my daily transfer limit, so I can't send more.
한도가 넘다 = exceed the cap; a very common banking snag
은행 앱에 로그인하면 바로 이체할 수 있어요.
Once you log in to the bank app, you can transfer right away.
이체하다 = to transfer between accounts; simplified to everyday app login
nuance: 이체 (移替, 'shift-replace') means moving money from one account to another and almost always appears as 계좌 이체 on bank apps and ATM screens. It overlaps heavily with 송금, and the sharp dividing line is perspective: 이체 stresses the account-to-account mechanics (the money relocates between 계좌), whereas 송금 stresses the act of remitting TO a person. Both take 하다. Do not, however, blur it with 입금 (depositing money INTO an account) — 이체 is the lateral move, 입금 is the inflow. Common collocations: 계좌 이체, 이체 한도, 자동이체. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'transfer' as one undifferentiated word and forgetting the 이체 한도 — a daily ceiling banks set low on new accounts, which silently blocks a large one-time transfer until you raise it.

usage: 환전 + 하다; the thing you swap into takes 로 (달러로 환전하다)
소 (所) = place; the manned booth where you swap cash
수수료 (手數料) varies by booth, so it pays to compare
환율 (換率) is the rate; 좋다/나쁘다 describe a favorable/poor rate
examples: 여행 가기 전에 환전했어요.
I exchanged money before going on the trip.
simple time-clause ~기 전에 = 'before doing'
공항에서 환전하면 환율이 안 좋아요.
If you exchange at the airport, the rate is bad.
distinguishes 환전 (the act) from 환율 (the rate) in one breath
명동 환전소가 은행보다 수수료가 싸다고 해서 거기서 바꿨어요.
I heard the Myeongdong booths charge lower fees than banks, so I changed it there.
real situation; note casual 바꾸다 standing in for 환전하다
nuance: 환전 (換錢, literally 'exchange-money') is swapping one currency for another — won into dollars before a trip home, say — and takes 하다, with the target currency marked by 로 (달러로 환전하다). Keep three look-alikes apart: 환전 is the ACT of changing currency, 환율 (換率) is the exchange RATE you get, and 환불 (還拂) is a totally separate word meaning a refund. In casual speech 돈을 바꾸다 ('change money') often substitutes for 환전하다. Collocations: 해외 환전, 환전 수수료, 환율이 좋다/나쁘다. The English-speaker pitfall is letting 'exchange' collapse 환전 and 환율 into one — and confusing 환전 with the unrelated 환불 — so anchor 환전 to the action and remember each bank or 환전소 sets its own 수수료, which is why where you exchange genuinely matters.

usage: 부족하다 (不足) — the exact phrase on decline messages
확인하다 (確認) is the standard verb for checking a figure
the amount sitting in your 통장
조회 (照會) is the menu wording at ATMs and in apps
examples: 지금 잔액이 얼마예요?
How much is the balance right now?
simple 얼마예요 question about an amount
교통카드 잔액이 천 원밖에 안 남았어요.
My transit card only has 1,000 won left.
shows 잔액 used for a transit card; ~밖에 + negative = 'only'
카드 결제가 안 돼요. 통장 잔액이 부족한가 봐요.
The card won't go through — I guess the account balance is low.
real checkout moment; ~(으)ㄴ가 봐요 = 'I guess/it seems'
nuance: 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining-amount') is the money left over — in your 통장, on a credit card, or on a 교통카드 (transit card) — and you'll hear the recorded line 잔액이 부족합니다 constantly when a payment is declined, so learn it by ear. Distinguish it crisply from 잔돈 (殘돈): 잔액 is the balance remaining in an account, while 잔돈 is the loose CHANGE handed back after you pay cash. The casual phrasing 남은 돈 ('money left') exists in speech, but formal banking contexts — ATMs, apps, tellers — expect 잔액. Collocations: 잔액 부족, 잔액 조회, 통장 잔액. usage: 입금 + 하다; you 입금하다 into an account marked with 에
확인 (確認) — sellers ask for this to verify the money landed
무 (無) = without; paying into an account via ATM with no book
for a deposit to go through
되다 is intransitive — money arrives on its own (입금됐어요)
examples: 방금 입금했어요.
I just made the deposit.
방금 (just now) + the past tense is the quick 'it's done' line
돈 보냈는데 입금 확인 좀 해 주세요.
I sent the money, so please confirm the deposit.
exact phrase buyers say to sellers in online deals
보증금은 계약하는 날 집주인 계좌로 입금하면 돼요.
You can pay the deposit into the landlord's account on the day you sign.
real housing situation; 계좌로 입금하다 + ~면 되다 ('it's fine to')
nuance: 입금 (入金, literally 'enter-money') is money going INTO an account, the exact opposite of 출금 (出金, 'exit-money') — picture the 入 character as funds stepping in. It takes 하다 when you do it, but note the key voice split: 입금하다 is what YOU actively do, while 입금되다 (intransitive) is what happens when money arrives on its own. Sellers and landlords constantly request 입금 확인 to verify your payment landed, and 무통장 입금 ('passbook-less deposit') is the normal ATM phrase for paying into someone's account. Collocations: 입금 확인, 무통장 입금, 보증금 입금. The English-speaker pitfall is direction (입금 in vs 출금 out) and, above all, saying 입금받다 — for money simply arriving the natural form is 입금되다 (입금됐어요), reserving 받다 for receiving a physical thing.

usage: 출금 + 하다; you 출금하다 from an account marked with 에서
한도 (限度) — the daily cap, set low on new accounts
현금 (現金) = cash; the most common reason to 출금
for a withdrawal to be blocked
안 되다 covers limits, fraud holds, or low balance
examples: ATM에서 오만 원 출금했어요.
I withdrew 50,000 won from the ATM.
ATM에서 marks the source point of the cash
새 통장은 하루 출금 한도가 정해져 있어요.
A new account has a set daily withdrawal limit.
정해져 있다 = 'is set'; explains why big withdrawals get blocked
밤 열한 시에 다른 은행 ATM에서 출금하면 수수료가 붙어요.
If you withdraw at 11 p.m. from another bank's ATM, a fee is added.
real after-hours scenario; 수수료가 붙다 = 'a fee attaches'
nuance: 출금 (出金, literally 'exit-money') is taking money OUT of an account, the natural pair to 입금 (入金, 'enter-money') — the 出 character even pictures funds leaving. It takes 하다, and the source account is marked with 에서 (통장에서 출금하다). It headlines every ATM screen and app menu. Crucially, fraud-protection rules give brand-new accounts a low 출금 한도, so a large withdrawal may be refused until you raise the cap at a branch. Collocations: 현금 출금, 출금 한도, 출금 수수료. nuance: 자동이체 (自動移替, literally 'self-moving transfer') is a standing instruction that pulls a fixed amount from your account on a set schedule — 월세, phone, utility bills — built from 자동 (自動, automatic) plus 이체 (移替, account transfer). That's the sharp contrast with a plain 이체: an 이체 is a single manual move you trigger each time, whereas 자동이체 runs by itself once registered. The idiomatic verb is 빠져나가다 ('slip out'), as in 자동이체로 빠져나가요. Collocations: 자동이체 신청/등록, 자동이체 설정. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming, as with a Western auto-pay, that the system covers a shortfall — it does not: if your 잔액 is short on the due date, the 자동이체 simply fails (안 됐어요) with no overdraft, so you must keep enough money in the account.

nuance: 대출 (貸出, literally 'lend-out') is a bank loan: you 받다 (receive/take out) one and later 갚다 (pay it back) together with 이자 (利子), the interest. Mind two boundaries. First, against 대여 (貸與): 대출 is specifically borrowing MONEY from a financial institution, whereas 대여 leans toward lending or renting OBJECTS (책 대여, 장비 대여). Second, on the paperwork, keep 이자 (ongoing interest on the principal) apart from 수수료 (a one-time service charge). For residents the headline product is a 전세 대출, a loan covering a housing deposit, which banks advertise heavily. Collocations: 대출을 받다/갚다, 대출 이자, 전세 대출. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: a loan is 받다 (received), and you don't '하다' a 대출 the way English 'take a loan' might tempt you — and never confuse 대출 with the object-renting 대여.
